strengths: The paper derives a self-consistent dynamical mean-field theory for linear/kernel regression with power-law-distributed kernel spectra using the MSRDJ formalism combined with a variational Gaussian approximation, providing a clean, compact description in terms of only two self-averaging order parameters (the trace of the response function and the autocorrelation, the latter directly proportional to the test error), which is fewer and more interpretable than the auxiliary fields used in closely related prior work (Bordelon et al., 2024).

The framework genuinely unifies several regimes studied separately in the literature: Bayesian inference on Gaussian processes (t→∞, finite β), gradient flow with/without weight decay (β→∞), and stochastic Langevin dynamics, with the Bayesian interpretation of the Langevin temperature spelled out explicitly in Appendix F.

Quantitative theory-experiment agreement is demonstrated across all figures: mode-wise learning dynamics (Fig. 1), test-error trajectories at multiple noise levels (Fig. 2), bias-variance decomposition (Fig. 3), and the effect of regularization on the early-stopping minimum (Fig. 4), with disorder averages over 10^5 realizations of training data.

The mechanistic explanation of early stopping as a temporal bias-variance trade-off — with the effective disorder-induced colored noise (Eq. 20/59) driving the growing variance term and the collective memory kernel K (an Onsager-reaction-like self-coupling) governing the slowdown and bias decay — is a clear, physically interpretable contribution that connects spectral and dynamical properties.
The derivation in the appendices (resummation of the Wishart cumulant expansion, geometric series for the response function) is detailed and traceable, making the theory reproducible in principle.
Limitations are honestly discussed: the restriction to linearized/kernel settings is acknowledged and connected to ongoing work on feature learning.
weaknesses: The empirical validation is narrow: all simulations use P = N = 100 with a single power-law exponent (Λ_ij = i^{-3/2} δ_ij). The theory is claimed to be exact in the large-N limit (CLT justification of the VGA), but this claim is never tested at larger system sizes or multiple exponents γ, and no real datasets or realistic spectra are considered. The generality implied by the title and introduction is not matched by the breadth of experiments.

The introduction promises 'analytical results that relate the power-law exponent of the feature kernel, regularization, and early stopping time to obtain a minimal generalization gap', but the paper delivers self-consistent integral equations that must be solved numerically (discretized with dt = 10^-2 in the theory); no closed-form scaling law for the minimal gap or optimal stopping time as a function of γ is actually derived. This central claim is thus only partially supported.

The novelty is incremental relative to prior work: the setting is close to Krogh & Hertz (1990; 1992), Advani et al. (2020) (dynamics, but i.i.d. data), Maloney et al. (2022) (power-law spectra, but static), Canatar et al. (2021) (power-law kernel spectra, but infinite time), and especially Bordelon et al. (2024; 2025) (dynamics with power-law data in linear random feature models). The main advances — adding Langevin noise, weight decay, and a more compact order-parameter description — are meaningful but modest, and the qualitative phenomena (spectral bias, early stopping, bias-variance trade-off) are largely expected from these predecessors.

The title ('random feature regression') is somewhat misleading: the model is regression on fixed Gaussian eigenmode features with a prescribed power-law spectrum, not random features in the Rahimi–Recht sense with feature learning; the relation of the assumed Gaussian features to actual random feature models or trained-network kernels is only asserted, not demonstrated.

Several presentation issues reduce polish: equation (5) writes ζ_i(t)ζ_j(s) where the correlator should be evaluated at equal arguments; the equation of motion below Eq. (13) appears with a sign inconsistent with Eq. (14); a citation dated 2026 ('Coppola et al., 2026') is used to support a claim about the kernel limit; and notation for the teacher weights (\bar{w} vs w̄) and Γ(\bar{v}, v, \bar{\tilde{v}}, G) is inconsistently typeset in places.

No code or software release is mentioned; while the equations are complete, reproducing the self-consistent numerical solution requires nontrivial implementation effort, and details such as how the theory time discretization (dt = 10^-2) affects accuracy at short times are not discussed.

The claimed advantage of avoiding replicas is fine, but the variational Gaussian approximation's controlledness (beyond the informal CLT argument) is not established; it is unclear how the approximation behaves near the interpolation threshold or for heavy-tailed feature statistics outside the Gaussian model.

strengths: The paper develops a coherent dynamical mean-field theory (MSRDJ formalism plus a variational Gaussian approximation) for linear/kernel regression with power-law-distributed kernel eigenvalues, and the derivation in the appendices is carried out with care and sufficient detail to follow (disorder average via the Wishart cumulant-generating function, resummation of the response series, self-consistent equations for mean, response, and correlation).

The unification of several regimes (gradient flow with/without weight decay, stochastic Langevin dynamics, and the Bayesian/GP posterior at equilibrium) within one framework is genuinely useful, and the link between the Langevin noise β⁻¹ and label noise in the Bayesian interpretation (Section F) is a nice observation.

The bias-variance decomposition of the test error over training time, explaining early stopping as an interplay between monotone bias decay and growing variance, is an interpretable and practically relevant result, and the analysis of how regularization affects the variance but barely the location of the minimum is interesting.
Theory and simulation agree well in the presented figures (Figs. 1–4), including per-mode dynamics and bias/variance components, which supports the internal consistency of the formalism.
The claim that only two self-averaging order parameters (traces of response and correlation) are needed, fewer than in prior work (Bordelon et al.), if correct, is a real simplification.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the setting is linear/kernel regression, and the main ingredients (MSRDJ/dynamical mean-field theory, disorder averaging, power-law spectra, bias-variance dynamics of early stopping) exist in prior work (Krogh & Hertz 1990/1992, Advani et al. 2020, Canatar et al. 2021, Bordelon et al. 2024/2025, Maloney et al. 2022). The contribution is largely a recombination—adding L2 regularization and Langevin noise to a known setup—with incremental conceptual gain.

A headline claim in the introduction (third bullet: 'obtain analytical results that relate the power-law exponent of the feature kernel, regularization, and early stopping time to obtain a minimal generalization gap') is not actually delivered in the manuscript: the results on early stopping are presented numerically/qualitatively via Figures 2–4, with no closed-form analytical scalings for the minimal gap or the optimal stopping time as a function of γ, gβ, or P.

Validation is thin: all simulations use N = P = 100 with a purely synthetic power-law spectrum (Λij = i^{-3/2}δij), far from the regime the theory claims to describe (N, P → ∞), and there are no experiments on realistic data, real kernel spectra, larger scales, or varying the exponent γ. The claimed 'quantitative' explanation of scaling-law phenomenology is thus only demonstrated in a small toy setting.

The central justification that the variational Gaussian approximation becomes exact in the large-N limit ('the central limit theorem guarantees the Gaussianity of the process') is asserted rather than proven, and the accuracy of the VGA at finite N or near the interpolation threshold is not systematically studied; this matters because the key claims (effective noise statistics, response slowdown) rest on the VGA.

Title/abstract oversell: the paper is titled 'random feature regression' but analyzes linear regression on Gaussian features in the kernel/NNGP limit; no feature learning or random-feature nonlinearity is actually treated. The abstract's claim of a 'principled understanding of the typical behavior of generalization in Neural Network Gaussian process regression dynamics' overstates what a linear model with synthetic spectra shows about real networks.

The paper does not state the scaling-law exponent predictions one would expect from the title; 'neural scaling laws' appear mainly as motivation and in the noise-driven growth of the error at late times, not as derived power-law test-error decay E ∝ t^{-...} or P^{-...} curves. A reader looking for the promised link between spectral exponent and scaling exponents finds little.

Reproducibility is limited: no code is provided or referenced, several simulation details are incomplete (e.g., how w̄ is drawn, how the disorder average over 10^5 realizations was implemented, the numerical solution procedure for the self-consistent equations), and there are presentation sloppinesses ('principle components', 'were modes are pairwise', inconsistent notation gβ vs. ḡβ, Fig. 4 legend calling gβ the 'strength of the dynamic noise', a citation dated 2026, mismatched Bordelon et al. 2024/2025 references), suggesting the manuscript needed another careful pass.

The related-work positioning, while reasonably thorough, does not clearly articulate what new prediction of the present theory could not have been obtained by directly solving the linear ODE ∂t w = −Ω(w − w̄) + ζ mode-by-mode plus known static results; the added value of the full field-theoretic machinery relative to elementary spectral analysis of the linear dynamics is not convincingly demonstrated.

strengths: The paper develops a self-consistent dynamical mean-field theory (MSRDJ formalism combined with a variational Gaussian approximation) for L2-regularized linear/kernel regression under Langevin dynamics, unifying gradient flow, weight decay, stochastic Langevin training, and the Bayesian/GP posterior in a single framework. This is a genuine and useful technical contribution.

The derivation is carried out carefully, with the disorder-averaged action, order-parameter identification, resummation of the geometric series of response functions, and the effective stochastic equation of motion all worked out in detail in Appendices A-D. The resulting description in terms of two self-averaging order parameters (trace of the response and of the autocorrelation) is compact and interpretable, and the test error appears naturally as half the correlation order parameter.

The theory yields mechanistic insight: the disorder-induced memory kernel (an Onsager-reaction-like self-coupling) that slows learning of all modes, the emergence of a temporally correlated effective noise, and a dynamical bias-variance decomposition that explains early stopping as a temporal trade-off. The qualitative explanation of why regularization affects late-time variance but not the location of the minimum is interesting.
Simulations of the microscopic dynamics (Figs. 1-4) agree well with the theory over a range of noise strengths and regularization levels, supporting the derivation in the regimes tested.
The paper is honest about its scope: the discussion clearly states the restriction to linearized/kernel settings and identifies the extension to feature-learning networks as future work.
weaknesses: The central quantitative claim of the abstract/introduction - that the theory yields 'analytical results that relate the power-law exponent of the feature kernel, regularization, and early stopping time to obtain a minimal generalization gap' - is not clearly delivered in the manuscript. The main text presents mostly qualitative discussion of the bias-variance trade-off and numerical solution of the self-consistency equations; no closed-form relation between the spectral exponent, regularization, and optimal stopping time is derived or displayed.

Validation is limited to small systems (P = N = 100). The theory is claimed to be exact in the N -> infinity limit, but no experiment approaches this limit, and visible theory-simulation deviations occur precisely where they matter (late-time noise floor in Fig. 1, late-time mismatch in Fig. 2). A scaling study showing convergence with N would substantially strengthen the exactness claim for the VGA.

Novelty relative to prior work is incremental. The closest works (Krogh & Hertz 1992; Advani et al. 2020; Canatar et al. 2021; Bordelon et al. 2024/2025) already cover much of the phenomenology (spectral bias, early stopping, power-law spectra, kernel dynamics). The genuinely new elements - finite-temperature Langevin dynamics with L2 regularization and an explicit treatment of response functions - are valuable but modest additions, and the resulting scientific findings (early stopping exists; noise hurts; regularization helps at late times) are largely expected.

The claim that the variational Gaussian approximation becomes exact for large N via the central limit theorem is asserted rather than proven; the conditions under which self-averaging and the Gaussianity of the effective process hold (e.g., relative sizes of P and N, behavior at the interpolation threshold) deserve a more careful argument, particularly since experiments sit at P = N.

Several presentation issues reduce clarity: the notation w vs. w-bar is confusingly typeset in Eqs. (1)-(2) and (10); Eq. (29) sets L_test = 1/2 C-bar(t, s) with 's' undefined (should be t, t); Fig. 4's caption states beta = 100 while the axis labels use g-bar, creating ambiguity about which parameter is varied; and there are minor grammatical errors throughout.

No code or reproducibility artifacts are mentioned despite the results depending on numerical solution of self-consistent integral equations and an averaging procedure over 10^5 disorder realizations.

strengths: The paper derives a self-consistent dynamical mean-field theory (MSRDJ formalism plus variational Gaussian approximation) for Langevin/gradient-flow training of kernel regression with power-law spectra, unifying Bayesian GP inference, gradient flow with/without weight decay, and stochastic Langevin dynamics in a single framework with interpretable order parameters (R, C).

The theory recovers established results as limits: it reproduces Canatar et al. (2021) in the stationary noiseless case (Appendix I) and is consistent with Bordelon et al. (2024) in the appropriate regime, which lends credibility to the derivation.

The derivation that the disorder-averaged action induces decoupled mode dynamics coupled only through self-averaging memory kernels, and the argument (Appendix C) that the VGA becomes exact as N→∞ via Ito-convention cancellations, is careful and insightful; the identification of the Onsager-reaction-like self-coupling as the mechanism slowing learning is a nice interpretive contribution.

Concrete new quantitative results are obtained: the optimal stopping time t* = (β/2)·α/(1+α) independent of P and N, the conjugacy of sample size P and inverse temperature β in the optimal generalization error (37), and a full dynamical bias-variance decomposition explaining early stopping; these are validated against simulations with substantial disorder averaging (up to 10^5 realizations).

The paper is honest about limitations (restriction to linearized/lazy settings, finite-size effects, the t→∞ difficulty at finite P) and outlines credible extensions (label noise in Section H, committee machines in Section J).
weaknesses: Incremental novelty relative to closely related work: Bordelon, Atanasov & Pehlevan (2024) already studied gradient-flow dynamics with power-law data in random feature models, and Paquette et al. derived Volterra-equation descriptions for SGD with power-law features. The main additions—L2 regularization, Langevin noise, and fewer order parameters—refine rather than fundamentally change the picture, and the headline scaling exponents (−α/(1+α) in Pt, N^{−α}) coincide with known results.

The distinctive feature of the theory—the collective memory kernel K mediating disorder-induced slowdown—is discarded in the derivations of the scaling laws (Section G replaces K ≈ δ(t−s), i.e., the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck approximation). Consequently, the quantitative early-stopping and scaling-law predictions do not actually exercise the paper's central mechanism; the authors only note the true bias 'will decay slower'. This weakens the link between the sophisticated mean-field machinery and the concrete results reported.

The claimed exactness of the VGA in the N→∞ limit is argued via perturbative/subleading-term heuristics (Appendix C) rather than a rigorous proof, and the analytic continuation of Γ(−1/(1+α), ·) in Appendix G.2 is glossed over.

Simulation scales are modest (mostly N = P = 100, one experiment at N = 1000) for a theory whose quantitative claims are thermodynamic-limit statements; finite-size effects are acknowledged but the N^{−α} corrections are said to be significant, leaving the agreement partly qualitative.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: β simultaneously controls Langevin noise and, through gβ, the regularization strength (entangled by construction, though g is tuned in figures); notation wavers between ηi and Λij across text and figure captions; Figure 2's caption and in-text discussion (Fig. 2a vs 2b) are inconsistent; there are scattered typos and a forward-dated citation (Coppola et al., 2026).

The early-stopping result t* ∝ β relies on the high-noise β-dependent variance dominating and on the OUP approximation; its robustness outside this regime and its relevance to realistic (non-Langevin) training is not established.

strengths: The paper develops a self-consistent dynamical mean-field theory (MSRDJ formalism + variational Gaussian approximation) for Langevin/kernel regression dynamics with power-law spectra, and the appendix derivation (Sections A–D) is reasonably careful, including a discussion of why subleading cross-mode couplings vanish in the N→∞ limit.

The unification is genuine and useful: the same framework covers gradient flow (β→∞), weight decay, and Langevin dynamics, and the stationary limit is explicitly shown to recover the static kernel-regression results of Canatar et al. (2021), including the γ renormalization factor — a solid consistency check.

The temporal bias–variance decomposition of the test error (Eq. 32) and the resulting early-stopping analysis is a clear and interpretable contribution; the prediction that the optimal stopping time t* ∝ β is independent of both P and N (Eq. 36) is a crisp, falsifiable claim supported by simulation (Fig. 5).
The role of the disorder-induced memory kernel K as an effective self-coupling/Onsager reaction term that slows down learning is an interesting dynamical insight beyond purely static treatments.
Limitations are acknowledged honestly: the setting is restricted to linearized/kernel regimes, and finite-size effects on the optimal loss are admitted (Fig. 4).
weaknesses: The headline scaling-law results (Section 5, Eqs. 33–37) are not derived from the paper's main theoretical machinery. They are obtained in the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck limit where the disorder of Q is discarded (K ≈ δ(t−s)), i.e., precisely the collective memory kernel that the DMFT was built to capture is switched off. The bias law (34) largely reproduces known results (Bordelon et al. 2024, Eq. 125), so the genuinely new predictions rest on the simplest approximation rather than the framework's core contribution.

The early-stopping result t* = β α/(2(1+α)) is derived in the high-noise (β→0) regime under the OUP approximation, where the variance power law (35) is only a transient (the exact OUP variance saturates at N/(2Pβ)). The paper presents this independence of P and N as a general conclusion without clearly delineating its regime of validity.

The empirical validation is weak for a theory whose regime is N→∞: simulations use N = P = 100 (at most N = 1000 in Fig. 4), and the paper itself concedes that N^{−α} corrections 'cannot be neglected' and that finite-size effects matter for estimating the optimal error. No systematic finite-size scaling study is provided.

Novelty is incremental. Relative to Bordelon, Atanasov & Pehlevan (2024), which already studies dynamical scaling laws with power-law data in linear random-feature models, the additions are Langevin noise, L2 regularization, and the response-function analysis; the VGA methodology is imported from Helias & Dahmen (2020). The paper does not clearly quantify what new phenomena (as opposed to reformulations) the extra machinery yields.

Presentation issues undermine confidence: β is heavily overloaded (Langevin temperature, appearing inside the regularization scale gβ, and in kernel definitions), several figure captions are confusing or inconsistent (e.g., Fig. 2a lists β = 10000/50/10 while the color legend reads β = 10/50/10000; Fig. 3 caption has 'β = 100,' with stray formatting), the unexplained factor 6 in the compute f = 6PNt, and typos in equations (e.g., 'P η' vs. 'P ηi', broken subscripts in (75)).

No code or additional reproducibility material is mentioned, and the 'a posteriori' argument that the variational Gaussian ansatz becomes exact is asserted rather than rigorously established, which matters given that the paper's quantitative claims depend on it.

The claimed link to 'random feature regression' and real networks is thinner than the title suggests: the theory is linear regression on Gaussian features with prescribed power-law spectrum; no experiment on actual kernels or trained-network features is provided, so the empirical relevance of the predicted exponents remains untested.

strengths: The paper derives a self-consistent dynamical mean-field theory (MSRDJ + variational Gaussian approximation) for Langevin training dynamics in kernel regression with power-law spectra, unifying Bayesian GP inference, gradient flow with/without weight decay, and stochastic Langevin dynamics within a single framework — a genuinely useful consolidation of previously separate lines of work.

The theory yields interpretable order parameters (response function and parameter autocorrelation, the latter directly proportional to the test error), and the derivation is detailed and largely self-contained: the disorder-averaged action, the equations of state, the resummation of the geometric series for the memory kernel K, and the effective equations of motion are all given explicitly in Appendices A–D.

Important sanity checks are provided: the stationary limit is shown in Appendix I to exactly recover Canatar et al. (2021), and the P,t → ∞ bias scaling recovers Bordelon et al. (2024); this substantially increases confidence in the correctness of the derivation.

The scaling-law analysis produces concrete, quantitative predictions: the bias decays as (Pt)^{-α/(1+α)} with an N^{-α} correction, the variance grows as β^{-1}P^{-α/(1+α)}t^{1/(1+α)}, and the optimal stopping time t* = (β/2)·α/(1+α) is independent of both P and N, with the conjugacy of sample size and inverse temperature (P·β). These predictions are verified against direct simulations with substantial disorder averaging (10^3–10^5 realizations), and theory and simulation agree well in the figures.

The mechanism-level explanations are valuable: the disorder-induced memory kernel acting as an Onsager-like reaction term that slows all modes collectively, and the temporal bias-variance decomposition explaining early stopping and the limited effect of L2 regularization on the location of the minimum test error.
Appendix H extends the framework to static label noise and Appendix J sketches an extension to committee machines, indicating the formalism is not tied to the single linear case.
The paper honestly discusses limitations, acknowledging restriction to linearized/lazy settings and that feature learning requires future work.
weaknesses: The headline scaling-law results (Section 5, Eqs. 33–37, and the early-stopping predictions) are not derived from the full mean-field theory developed in Section 4 but from the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck approximation in which the memory kernel is replaced by K ≃ δ(t−s), i.e., the disorder of Q is neglected. This is an internal tension: the paper's central technical achievement is the disorder-induced collective memory kernel and the resulting slowdown of learning, yet the quantitative power-law claims deliberately discard exactly this effect. The derived exponents are therefore bounds/asymptotic limits, and the claimed relation between the kernel exponent, regularization, early stopping time, and minimal generalization gap is only established in this approximated regime.

Validation is restricted to small synthetic systems (N, P ≈ 100–1000) with Gaussian i.i.d. features and a noiseless teacher. There are no experiments on real data or real kernel spectra, so the applicability of the predictions to the neural scaling laws that motivate the paper (Kaplan et al.) remains speculative; the claim of quantitative explanation rests on agreement within the same idealized model class as the theory.

The contribution over closely related prior work — particularly Bordelon, Atanasov & Pehlevan (2024), who already study gradient-flow dynamics with power-law data in linear random feature models — is incremental: the main additions are Langevin (finite-temperature) noise, L2 regularization, and a bias-variance/early-stopping analysis. The authors' stated advantages (fewer, more interpretable order parameters; inclusion of L2) are real but modest, and the most novel quantitative results rely on the approximation discussed above.

Presentation issues reduce clarity and reproducibility: the power-law exponent is introduced as γ in Eq. (9) (η_i = η1 i^{−1−γ}) but the text thereafter uses α without comment; in Eqs. (1)–(2) teacher and student weights are both typeset as w (distinguishing bar is lost); symbols for the prefactor P·η_i are inconsistently typeset (Pη_k, Pη, P ηi); and several equations contain minor typographical slips. Figure captions are dense but the simulation protocol (code availability, numerical solvers for the self-consistent equations) is not described, and no code release is mentioned.

The variance scaling L_β ∝ t^{1/(1+α)} is derived under assumptions (β → 0, weak regularization, OUP limit) whose window of validity is not delineated — in particular, when and how the growth saturates, and how the OUP-based variance behaves once the full memory kernel matters at late times. The authors note finite-size effects are important (Fig. 4) but the regime boundaries are not systematically mapped.

The self-consistency loop (C̄ requires ⟨δvδv⟩ which requires C̄) is solved numerically, but the paper does not specify how (discretization of the coupled convolution equations, convergence behavior, cost), which hampers independent reproduction of the 'theory' curves.

The Gaussianity of features is a strong assumption that in principle changes the Wishart structure and hence the entire disorder term; the paper asserts (via cited recent work) that kernel-limit results transfer to real data but provides no direct evidence within the paper itself.
